idea.body: Adding or subtracting decimals works like whole numbers once the decimal points line up. Write one number under the other so the decimal points sit in the same column. Fill any missing decimal digit with a zero, so both numbers reach the same length. Add or subtract from the right, carrying or borrowing exactly as you would without a decimal point at all. Then drop the decimal point straight down into the answer. A kitchen scale reading 3.6 kilograms plus another reading 2.75 kilograms: write 3.60 under 2.75, add the columns, and the total is 6.35 kilograms.

figure.alt: A bar picture of 3.6: three full bars of ten squares, and a fourth bar with six of ten squares shaded.

workedExample.prompt: A rover logs 4.8 kilometers on one day and 3.65 kilometers on the next. What is the two-day total?
steps: Line up the decimal points: 4.80 above 3.65.
Write 4.8 as 4.80 so both numbers have two decimal digits.
Add the hundredths: 0 plus 5 is 5.
Add the tenths: 8 plus 6 is 14, write 4 and carry 1.
Add the ones, plus the carry: 4 plus 3 plus 1 is 8.
The total is 8.45 kilometers.

figure.alt: A bar picture of 4.8: four full bars of ten squares, and a fifth bar with eight of ten squares shaded.

ways.name: Stack and align
ways.when: Use this for any decimal addition or subtraction, especially with pen and paper.
steps: Write one number under the other so the decimal points line up in the same column.
Fill any missing decimal digit with a zero so both numbers reach the same length.
Add or subtract from the right, carrying or borrowing as with whole numbers.
Drop the decimal point straight down into the answer.
ways.trap: Lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points, when the numbers have different lengths.

ways.name: Scale to whole numbers
ways.when: Use this when thinking in whole numbers feels easier than tracking a decimal point.
steps: Multiply both numbers by 100, or whatever clears every decimal digit.
Add or subtract the whole numbers that result.
Divide the answer by that same amount.
That gives the decimal answer.
ways.trap: Multiplying the two numbers by different amounts instead of the exact same power of ten.

ways.name: Split whole and decimal parts
ways.when: Use this when doing the sum in your head, without writing anything down.
steps: Add or subtract the whole number parts first.
Add or subtract the decimal parts on their own.
If the decimal part reaches 1 or more, carry 1 into the whole number total.
Combine the two results for the final answer.
ways.trap: Forgetting to carry the extra 1 into the whole number when the decimal parts add past 1.

ways.name: Jump along a number line
ways.when: Use this for subtraction, especially finding the gap between two measurements.
steps: Start at the smaller number.
Jump up to the next friendly whole number first.
Jump in easy chunks up to the larger number.
Add up every jump you made; that total is the answer.
ways.trap: Losing track of one small jump and leaving it out of the final total.

figure.alt: A number line from 2.75 to 6.35 with three jumps above it: plus 0.25, plus 3.00, and plus 0.35.

frames.caption: Jump to the next whole number.
Jump in chunks to the larger number.
Add up every jump for the total.

bank.prompt: A rover logs the distance it drives each day, in kilometers. One entry reads 3.2 km and the next reads 4.5 km. What is the total, in kilometers?
explanation: Line up the decimal points so tenths sit under tenths and hundredths under hundredths.
Add each column from the right: 3.2 plus 4.5 gives 7.7.
Check the total by rounding both numbers to the nearest whole and seeing the sum lands close.
bank.useAgain: when you add two decimal amounts that do not have the same number of decimal digits.
hints: Line up the decimal points first, one under the other, before you add anything.
Pad any missing places with a zero. Then add column by column from the right, carrying when a column reaches ten.
bank.socraticHint: If you moved the decimal point of one number before adding, would the columns still be adding the same kind of place value?

After the loss: 18.35 minus 5.4 is 12.95.
After the second gain: 12.95 plus 2.05 is 15.
Each step uses the running total from the step before it, never the original starting value.
stretch.useAgain: when a reading changes several times in a row and you need the value after all of them.
hints: Work through the changes strictly in the order they happened.
Use the result of each step as the starting point for the next one, not the very first number.
stretch.socraticHint: Does the final reading depend on the order the gains and the loss happened in?

stretch.useAgain: when a total and one part give you a second amount, and a third amount is defined from that second one.
